article.h1: Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test: A 6-Question Self-Quiz and What Your Result Means
article.body_html:
A Fitzpatrick skin type test is a short self-quiz that sorts you into one of six types, I to VI, based on your natural coloring and how your skin tends to react to sun. Answer from memory about untreated skin, tally the numbers, and treat the result as a rough category, not a medical assessment.

This guide gives you a quiz you can finish in a couple of minutes, explains what each type describes, and shows where the scale helps and where it doesn't. It also covers how to use the result for cosmetic decisions such as makeup and color choices. The quiz is a self-guided, informal tool for style and education only.

What is the Fitzpatrick skin type scale?

The Fitzpatrick scale is a six-point system that groups skin by its natural coloring and its typical reaction to sun, from Type I (very fair, burns easily, rarely tans) to Type VI (deeply pigmented, rarely burns). It describes a broad pattern, not your exact shade or undertone.

The six types (I to VI) in plain language

  • Type I: very fair skin that burns easily and typically does not tan.
  • Type II: fair skin that burns easily and tans only slightly.
  • Type III: light to medium skin that sometimes burns and tans gradually.
  • Type IV: olive or light brown skin that burns only a little and tans easily.
  • Type V: medium to deep brown skin that rarely burns and tans darkly.
  • Type VI: deep brown to very deep skin that very rarely burns.

If you searched for a Fitzpatrick skin types chart or "skin type 1 to 6", that list is the short version. Note that this is a different use of "skin type" than oily, dry or combination.

What the scale measures: how skin tends to react to sun

At its core, the scale is about reaction: does your skin tend to burn, tan, or both, and how quickly? That is why the quiz below leans on memories of past sun exposure, not on how your skin looks today.

What the scale does not measure: undertone, shade, or skin health

The scale does not tell you whether your undertone is warm, cool or neutral. It does not give you a foundation shade, and it says nothing about the condition of your skin. Two people with the same type can look quite different side by side.

How do I set up to answer honestly?

Think about your skin as it naturally is, without self-tanner, recent tanning or products, and answer based on what usually happens, not one unusual day.

Think about untreated skin and typical reactions

Check a spot that rarely sees the sun, such as the inner upper arm. For hair and eye color, answer for your natural coloring, not dye or colored contacts. If you can't remember how your skin reacted to sun, pick the answer that fits best and note that your result is less certain.

Use natural light and a bare face

Judge your natural coloring near a window in daylight, away from colored walls and warm bulbs. Indoor lighting can push skin looking more yellow, pink or gray than it really is.

Why memory-based answers are only approximate

The test relies on recalling past reactions, and memory is imperfect. Sunscreen use, shade, season and time of day all change what happened, so keep your expectations modest.

Fitzpatrick skin type test: a 6-question self-quiz

For each question, pick the answer that fits best and write down its number (1 to 6). The scoring method is a simple informal one for self-reflection, not a clinical instrument.

Questions 1 to 3: natural coloring

1. What is your natural skin color on a rarely exposed area?

  • Very pale or ivory = 1
  • Fair = 2
  • Light to medium beige = 3
  • Olive or light brown = 4
  • Medium to deep brown = 5
  • Deep to very deep brown = 6

2. What is your natural eye color? (A weak clue, so don't over-weigh it.)

  • Light blue, gray or green = 1
  • Blue, green or hazel = 2
  • Hazel or light brown = 3
  • Brown = 4
  • Dark brown = 5
  • Brownish-black = 6

3. What was your natural hair color before any dye or graying?

  • Red or very light blond = 1
  • Blond = 2
  • Light or medium brown = 3
  • Dark brown = 4
  • Very dark brown = 5
  • Black = 6

Questions 4 to 6: sun reaction

4. After a first extended stretch of unprotected sun, what usually happens?

  • Always burns, often painfully, and peels = 1
  • Burns easily and usually peels = 2
  • Sometimes burns mildly = 3
  • Rarely burns = 4
  • Very rarely burns = 5
  • Almost never burns = 6

5. How does your skin tend to tan?

  • Doesn't tan, just freckles or turns red = 1
  • Tans lightly or barely = 2
  • Tans gradually to a light brown = 3
  • Tans easily to a moderate brown = 4
  • Tans very easily to a dark brown = 5
  • Deepens to a very deep brown naturally = 6

6. How quickly does color deepen, and how long does it last?

  • No visible change = 1
  • Slight change that fades quickly = 2
  • Gradual change over days to weeks = 3
  • Visible within a day or two = 4
  • Very quick and lasts a long time = 5
  • Change is hard to see because skin is already deep = 6

How to tally your answers, and what to do with a tie

Add your six numbers, divide by six and round to the nearest whole number. That is your rough type. If you land between two types, such as 3.5, lean on questions 4 to 6, since the scale is built around sun reaction. If you're still undecided, describe yourself as "between III and IV". That is a perfectly reasonable answer.

What do my results mean?

Your result places you in a broad group of people whose skin tends to react to sun in a similar way. For style purposes, it is background context, not a final label.

Types I and II

These types usually have fair skin that burns easily, often with lighter eyes and hair, though not always. Fair skin often shows redness or contrast more visibly, which can matter when you choose blush intensity or high-contrast outfits.

Types III and IV

These are the middle of the scale: light-to-medium or olive and light brown skin that tans more readily. This group covers an especially wide range of tones and undertones, which is why the number alone tells you little about foundation or palette.

Types V and VI

These types describe medium-deep to very deep skin that rarely burns. The scale is much less detailed here, so the range of shades and undertones in these two numbers is large.

Why your result is a rough category, not a precise label

Skin color changes with season and with how much sun you've had. The scale is coarse, so treat it as a rough starting category. This quiz is not medical advice. If you have concerns about your skin, moles, skin changes or how your skin reacts to sun, please see a dermatologist or doctor.

Is Fitzpatrick type the same as skin tone or undertone?

No. Fitzpatrick type describes sun reaction, depth describes how light or deep your skin is, and undertone describes the subtle warm, cool or neutral cast beneath the surface.

Sun reaction versus depth versus undertone, side by side

TermWhat it describesUseful for
Fitzpatrick typeTendency to burn or tanBackground context
DepthHow light or deep your skin looksFoundation range, contrast level
UndertoneWarm, cool or neutral castFoundation tone, clothing and makeup colors

Why two people with the same type can need different foundation or palettes

Imagine two people who both score a III. One has a golden, peachy undertone and looks best in warm olive green or camel. The other has a rosy undertone and may prefer cool berry or navy. The number is identical, but their color choices differ because undertone does most of the work.

Where the scale falls short, especially for deeper skin tones

The scale lumps a very wide range of deeper skin tones into a few numbers, so it isn't a good guide to shade or undertone for those groups. It also depends on memory and self-report. For picking colors, depth and undertone give you far more to work with.

To work those out, see our guide to finding your skin depth and undertone, or try the simple checks in what color undertones you have.

How can I use this for makeup and color choices?

Start with undertone and depth, and treat your Fitzpatrick number as loose context only. It can nudge decisions, such as how bold to go with contrast, but it shouldn't pick your shade.

Start from undertone and depth

A practical rule of thumb: match foundation to your depth, then to your undertone. For clothing, warm undertones often suit olive, rust, cream and mustard, while cool undertones often suit navy, emerald, plum and true white. Neutral undertones can usually wear both. These are tendencies, not laws.

Test foundation and clothing colors in natural light

Swatch foundation along the jawline and check it in daylight after a few minutes, since some formulas shift as they settle. For clothes, hold a garment under your chin near a window. If your face looks brighter and your skin looks even, it's likely working. If you look tired or washed out, try a different shade.

Treat any palette advice as a starting point

Personal taste, hair color, eye color and the occasion all matter. If you want to preview lipstick or other looks before committing, our makeup virtual try-on guide shows how to do it usefully.

Where can a camera-based tool fit in, and where can't it?

A camera tool can help with the cosmetic step after the quiz, but it can't give you a Fitzpatrick type. FitCheck does not assign one, assess sun sensitivity or screen skin.

What FitCheck's live skin analysis offers

The live skin analysis feature uses your camera to give an AI skin overview with cosmetic beauty suggestions. Use it as a second opinion on tone and undertone as you think about makeup. The FitCheck app also has an AI makeup assistant and a live virtual makeup try-on, so you can preview something like a lipstick on your own face. Feedback is AI opinion, not a professional color analysis, and it is a starting point, not a verdict. A few optional AI features, such as hairstyle previews and AI try-on images, send the photo you choose to a third-party AI service to generate the result.

What it does not do

It does not diagnose, detect or treat any skin condition, and it is not medical advice. If you have any concern about your skin, see a dermatologist or doctor.

Photo tips

  • Face natural light, such as a window.
  • Hold the camera at eye level.
  • Avoid filters, which change how your skin color appears.

When should I talk to a dermatologist or doctor?

Talk to one for anything health-related, including changes in your skin, a mole that concerns you, or questions about how your skin reacts to sun.

Anything health-related

A style quiz can't tell you whether a spot or change is a concern. If something looks new, different or worrying, book an appointment instead of relying on a quiz.

Why a quiz or an app cannot replace a professional

Both the quiz and any app rely on limited information: your memory in one case, a photo in the other. A professional can examine your skin properly, which neither can do.

A clear note

This article and the AI feedback in FitCheck are for cosmetic and style guidance only, not medical advice. For any skin concern, please see a dermatologist or doctor.

faqs.question: Can my Fitzpatrick skin type change?
faqs.answer: The scale is meant to describe your general tendency, so it isn't supposed to change from week to week. Your visible skin color can shift with seasons and sun exposure, which may make your answers feel different at different times. If your answers fall between two types, it's fine to note both.

faqs.question: Does Fitzpatrick type tell me my undertone?
faqs.answer: No. Fitzpatrick type is about how skin tends to react to sun, while undertone is the warm, cool or neutral cast beneath the surface. People with the same type can have different undertones, so use separate undertone checks for makeup and color choices.

faqs.question: Is the Fitzpatrick scale the same as the skin tone charts used for makeup?
faqs.answer: No. Makeup shade ranges are built around depth and undertone and usually have many more steps than six. The Fitzpatrick scale is a coarse grouping, so it is a weak guide for picking a foundation shade.

faqs.question: Can an app tell me my Fitzpatrick type?
faqs.answer: Not reliably, and FitCheck doesn't try to. The scale depends on how your skin reacts to sun over time, which a photo can't show. FitCheck's live skin analysis offers a cosmetic overview with beauty suggestions, and it is not medical advice.

factual_issues: The quiz scoring is an invented averaging method (six 1-6 answers, divided by six). It is not the standard Fitzpatrick questionnaire, which uses weighted points across genetic traits, sun reaction and tanning habits. The article calls it informal, but the title 'Fitzpatrick Skin Type Test' and the 'your rough type' result imply more validity than it has.

Eye and hair color count as two of six equally weighted questions, which can skew results. A person with deep skin and light eyes, or fair skin and dark hair, will be pulled toward the wrong type. The text calls eye color a 'weak clue' but still gives it equal weight.

Q5 and Q6 (tanning and speed of color change) largely overlap. Q6's top option ('hard to see because skin is already deep = 6') is not a sun-reaction answer. Q2's answer options also overlap (hazel appears in both 2 and 3; 'blue, green' appears in both 1 and 2), so the quiz is ambiguous.

Type VI is described as 'very rarely burns' and Type V as 'rarely burns'. The usual descriptions are 'burns minimally' for IV and 'rarely/never burns' for VI, so the wording blurs the V/VI distinction.

The article does not say that every skin type can burn and develop skin cancer, or that the type should not be used to decide sun protection. Phrases like 'rarely burns' for Types V and VI could give a false sense of safety. Add a short sun-safety note.
'Use a bare face' is irrelevant to a sun-reaction recall quiz and slightly confusing.

review.notes: The article matches the informational intent well. It is clearly structured, explains that Fitzpatrick type differs from undertone and depth, and includes sound medical disclaimers and an honest statement that the app does not assign a Fitzpatrick type. It has no invented statistics or testimonials, and the privacy note about third-party AI is consistent with APP_FACTS. Fixes needed before publishing: (1) remove the tone/undertone claims about the app in the body and CTA; (2) add a sun-safety caveat that all skin types can burn and the result should not guide sun-protection decisions; (3) tidy the quiz by dropping or merging the overlapping Q5/Q6, removing option overlaps, and down-weighting or removing eye and hair color, or label it more clearly as a non-standard informal quiz; (4) correct the Type V/VI burn wording. Minor: verify that the internal links exist, and drop the 'bare face' point from the recall section.
